items.title: The Resilience of Uncertainty: How to Hold the Universe in You
items.description: “All things are so very uncertain, and that’s exactly what makes me feel reassured,” Tove Jansson wrote in one of our civilization’s great works of philosophy disguised as a children’s book. items.title: How to Be a Sea: Albert Camus on Learning to Die and Learning to Live
items.description: The summer I turned sixteen, I took a bus across Bulgaria — I suppose you could call it running away, though my parents were aware and unconcerned — to go sit on the edge of the Black Sea and watch the blue horizon, to touch its infinite loneliness and infinite happiness. I have watched many horizons in the lifetime since, and always they shimmer with the same strange duality, the same absolute awareness of mortality and of aliveness — the crest and trough of the same wave lapping at the essence

items.title: How Do You Know That You Love Somebody? Philosopher Martha Nussbaum’s Incompleteness Theorem of the Heart’s Truth, from Plato to Proust
items.description: "The alternations between love and its denial, suffering and denial of suffering … constitute the most essential and ubiquitous structural feature of the human heart."

items.title: How to Hold Death and Carry Life: A Zen Master Explains Existence to a Child and Outlines the Three Essential Principles of Zen Mind
items.description: "Zen practice ... requires great faith, great courage, and great questioning."

items.title: How to Read the Signal of Your Life
items.description: Sitting atop a Spanish mesa one sweltering August night, watching the Perseid meteor showers streak the sky with the debris of a comet burning through the atmosphere against the backdrop of a billion dead stars whose signal light is only now reaching us, I found myself trembling with the parallel to life itself: The great paradox is that we are aflame with aliveness only as we burn through the atmosphere of now, and yet our lives are the story we constellate from the signals of bygone experience

items.title: How to Bear Your Loneliness
items.description: "We are cheating ourselves when we run away from the ambiguity of loneliness."

items.title: The Loveliness of Letting Go: An Illustrated Ode to Life’s Lasts
items.description: The great cruelty of life, and also its great mercy, is that only hindsight ever knows each last — the last time your lover put their hand on the small of your back, the last sip of the last cup at your favorite coffee shop before it vanished overnight, the last living note of your mother’s voice. Bittersweet or downright devastating, lasts are the currency of loss with which we pay the price for loving. items.title: How to Be Un-Dead: Notes on Waking Up from the Trance of Near-Living
items.description: "Life is a process of becoming, a combination of states we have to go through. Where people fail is that they wish to elect a state and remain in it. This is a kind of death."

items.title: The Bird in the Heart: Terry Tempest Williams on the Paradox of Transformation and How to Live with Uncertainty
items.description: "We can change, evolve, and transform our own conditioning. We can choose to move like water rather than be molded like clay."

items.title: Moonlight and the Magic of the Unnecessary

items.title: Wilderness, Solitude, and Creativity: Artist and Philosopher Rockwell Kent’s Century-Old Meditations on Art and Life During Seven Months on a Small Alaskan Island
items.description: "These are the times in life — when nothing happens — but in quietness the soul expands."

items.title: How to Bear Your Desolations
items.description: "You may have to break your heart, but it isn’t nothing to know even one moment alive."

items.title: Where Love Goes When It Goes
items.description: This is an excerpt from Traversal. Where does love go when it goes? It is a common question, contrived in its commonness yet savagely sincere, bellowing in the bosom of every brokenhearted lover, reverberating through the body of every civilization’s love songs and sonnets, radiating from cave drawings and dive bar graffiti. items.title: The Other Significant Others: Living and Loving Outside the Confines of Conventional Friendship and Compulsory Coupledom
items.description: "While we weaken friendships by expecting too little of them, we undermine romantic relationships by expecting too much of them."

items.title: Georgia O’Keeffe on the Art of Seeing
items.description: "To see takes time, like to have a friend takes time."
